etymologies.etymologyHTML:
Attested in English since 1545, from French troupe (back-formation of troupeau, diminutive of Medieval Latin troppus "flock") and Middle French trouppe (from Old French trope (“band, company, troop”)), both of Germanic origin from Frankish *þorp (“assembly, gathering”), from Proto-Germanic *þurpą (“village, land, estate”), from Proto-Indo-European *treb- (“dwelling, settlement”).

Doublet of troupe, and possibly also of thorp, dorp, and trip. Cognate with German Dorf (“village”).

definitions.definition: (collective) A collection of people; a number; a multitude (in general).

quote.citation: c. 1606 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Macbeth”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene iii]:
quote.text: That which should accompany old age — / As honour, love, obedience, troops of friends — / I must not look to have.

definitions.definition: (military) A small unit of cavalry or armour commanded by a captain, corresponding to a platoon or company of infantry.
A detachment of soldiers or police, especially horse artillery, armour, or state troopers.
(chiefly in the plural) A group of soldiers; military forces.

quote.citation: c. 1591–1592 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Third Part of Henry the Sixt, […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i], page 147, column 2:
quote.text: Ah, knovv you not the Citie fauours them, / And they haue troupes of Souldiers at their beck?

quote.citation: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Othello, the Moore of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene iii]:
quote.text: Farewell the plumed troop, and the big wars.

quote.citation: 1849–1861, Thomas Babington Macaulay, chapter I, in The History of England from the Accession of James the Second, volume (please specify |volume=I to V), London: Longman, Brown, Green, and Longmans, →OCLC:
quote.text: His troops moved to victory with the precision of machines.

definitions.definition: (nonstandard) An individual soldier or member of a military force; a trooper.

quote.citation: 2018 August 8, Donald R. White, Death In a Lonely Place, Lulu.com, →ISBN, page 82:
quote.text: One American M48 was slightly grazed and one American troop lightly wounded.

quote.citation: (Can we date this quote?), Victor Grant-Lawrence, Conspiracy Theories And Stuff, Lulu.com, →ISBN:
quote.text: Although the mission failed, at least 5 ISIL militants were killed, however 1 American troop was wounded. According to the reports, Jordan had a role in the operation and that one Jordanian soldier had been wounded as well.

definitions.definition: (nonstandard) A company of actors; a troupe.

quote.citation: 1784, William Coxe, Travels into Poland, Russia, Sweden and Denmark:
quote.text: In order to form the new troop to a greater degree of perfection, the four principal actors were placed in the seminary of the cadets

definitions.definition: (scouting) A chapter of a national girl or boy scouts organization, consisting of one or more patrols of 6 to 8 youngsters each.
A group of meerkat families living together.
A particular roll of the drum; a quick march.
(mycology) A group of mushrooms that are close but not close enough to be called a cluster.
To move in numbers; to come or gather in crowds or troops.

quote.citation: 1918, W[illiam] B[abington] Maxwell, chapter V, in The Mirror and the Lamp, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: Then everybody once more knelt, and soon the blessing was pronounced. The choir and the clergy trooped out slowly,  […] , down the nave to the western door.  […]  At a seemingly immense distance the surpliced group stopped to say the last prayer.

definitions.definition: To march on; to go forward in haste.
To move or march as if in a crowd.
